clips.title: Evals Course: How to deal with nondeterminism
clips.why: A short, concrete look at the problem in the story: the same eval on the same data gives different scores, and the fix is to run it more than once.
look: Why the scores still move even with randomness turned down as far as it goes.
The fix in the eval tool: a trial count of 3, so every input runs three times and the results are averaged.
The real example at the end: one input scores A in one trial and B in the other two.
clips.after: Our record() makes the same choice as a hard rule: every case runs three times, and the spread between the rounds is stored next to the pass rate.

clips.title: OpenRouter Webinar: Cut Your AI Bill Without Cutting Quality
clips.why: Before comparing settings you need the right cost number: what a whole task costs, not what a token costs.
look: The difference between the price of one token and the cost of a whole task.
Why cost per task is the number to compare settings with.
Think of a setting that is cheaper per token but needs more turns: which number shows it?
clips.after: That is why the eval store keeps cost per case and median turns next to the pass rate: low effort only saves money if a whole task really costs less.

clips.title: OpenRouter Webinar: Cut Your AI Bill Without Cutting Quality
clips.why: People who run a service that routes requests across many models explain how evals help decide when a cheaper choice is good enough.
look: Listen for whose tasks the evals should use before you move to a cheaper choice: your own work, or public benchmarks.
Watch for quality and cost being read together, never one without the other.
Listen for how they decide that a cheaper option is good enough, and compare it with our low-edge rule.
clips.after: Our sweep is this idea with a fixed rule: the cheaper setting stays if its pass rate reaches the current setting's low edge, and a person approves the change in one pull request.

practice.q: A suite of 15 tasks passes 9, 12 and 11 tasks in its three rounds. What is its spread?

options.why: The spread is in pass rate, not in tasks. 3 tasks out of 15 is 20 points.
Best round 12 of 15 is 80%, worst round 9 of 15 is 60%. The spread is the difference between them.

options.text: About 7 points: one task out of 15
options.why: That is how much one task moves the score, not how far apart the best and worst rounds are.

practice.q: Finish the sweep's decision line so a cheaper setting is kept while it stays inside the current setting's wobble.
practice.before: keep_cheaper_if: its pass_rate >= current pass_rate - current
practice.hint: The best round minus the worst round.
practice.why: The current pass rate minus its spread is the low edge. Anything above it cannot be told apart from today's setting by this suite.

practice.q: Medium scores 78% with a spread of 4 points. High costs more and scores 84%. What does the rule say?

options.text: Move up to high: 84% clears the high edge of 82%.
options.why: A more expensive setting must beat the current pass rate by more than the spread. Here it does, so the extra cost buys a difference the suite can see.

options.text: Stay on medium: a more expensive setting is never chosen.
options.why: The sweep tries one level up on purpose. When a row loses quality on our code, it moves up.

options.text: Stay on medium: 6 points is inside the wobble.
options.why: The wobble here is only 4 points. With a small spread, a 6-point gain is real enough to count.

practice.q: Which split of BYTE-GOLD should the effort sweep run on?

options.text: holdout, because it gives the most honest number
options.why: The holdout is kept for the final check. If sweeps ran on it, settings would slowly be chosen to fit those cases, and the final check would stop being honest.

options.text: dev, the slice people work against every day
options.why: The sweep tunes settings, so it uses the working slice and leaves the holdout untouched.

options.text: Any split; the rule uses the spread, so it does not matter
options.why: The spread protects against luck, not against tuning to the cases. Which cases you tune on still matters.

practice.q: A new model ships. Put the new-model check in order.
items: Run each suite on the new model with every harness part on, three rounds: the reference
Switch off one part, with all the others on, and run three rounds again
Repeat for every other part, one at a time
Drop a part only if its pass rate stays above the reference's low edge and cost or time falls
Put the removals in the monthly pull request, and a person approves it
practice.why: The reference comes first, because every part-off run is judged against its low edge. One part at a time shows which part matters, and a person makes the final change.

practice.q: Finish the line in record() that computes the spread.
practice.hint: The best round minus the worst round.
practice.why: per_round holds the three rounds' pass rates. The spread is the highest minus the lowest.
